title: Opt-Out Odyssey
pitch: A roguelike gauntlet of invented websites, each greeting the visitor with a procedurally composed consent banner full of named tricks: a grey sliver where Reject should be, a countdown that resets, switches that mean the opposite of their label. The visitor hunts for the least-tracking outcome in the fewest clicks, then reads a debrief with the room's friction ratio (clicks to accept versus clicks to refuse), the par found by a built-in solver, and a bestiary entry for every pattern that fired. Eight rooms and a 300-vendor boss make a run, and a daily seed gives everyone the same gauntlet.
whyNow: Timeless: dismissing consent banners is a daily web chore (an observation, not a sourced statistic), and every figure on the page is dated and attributed, so nothing goes stale.

research.summary: A CHI 2020 paper (Nouwens and colleagues) analysed consent pop-ups from popular consent platforms on top UK websites and reported that only 11.8% met its minimal requirements based on European law; a later systematic review repeats the figure, and an MIT CSAIL news item headlines the finding. The denominator is unclear in the snippets, so the page would say 'in the study's sample'. Dark-pattern typologies are published by Canada's Office of Consumer Affairs and in a unified-taxonomy arXiv paper, giving named patterns for a bestiary. Cookie-banner games already exist (a Swiss broadcaster's browser game and a University of Luxembourg thesis game), so the edge is procedural variety, a solver-checked par and the friction ratio.

sources.note: Separate authors repeat the 11.8% figure; secondary, since it cites the primary study.

facts.claim: As of 2026-10-11, a CHI 2020 study (Nouwens and colleagues) of consent-platform pop-ups on top UK websites reported that only 11.8% met its minimal requirements based on European law; per the search summary the data are from 2019 and the denominator is unclear.

As of 2026-10-11, typologies of dark patterns are published by Canada's Office of Consumer Affairs ('Types of dark patterns') and in an arXiv paper titled '50 Shades of Deceptive Patterns: A Unified Taxonomy, Multimodal Detection, and Security Implications'.

As of 2026-10-11, cookie-banner games already exist: a Swiss broadcaster (SRF) published a browser game about finding the most data-sparing setting, and a University of Luxembourg master's thesis describes a five-level serious game called Dark Cookie.

Per blended search summaries, a widely used 2018 typology (Gray and colleagues) groups dark patterns into five categories: nagging, obstruction, sneaking, interface interference and forced action. Unverified.

Per one search result and its blended summary, the 2010 essay Can't Play, Won't Play by Margaret Robertson coined 'pointsification' for adding points and badges, which it calls the least essential part of games. Unverified.

The Hero's Journey as the room-by-room arc

design.coreLoop: Enter a room (an invented site with a seeded banner), read it under a patience timer, click through the layers to the lowest-tracking outcome, then read the debrief: trackers leaked, friction ratio, solver par and the named patterns that fired. Patience buys relics (contrast magnifier, one undo, tab-order sense) for the descent; every trap carries a visible tell, so each run sharpens the eye for the next, and bosses stack three patterns at once.
sophisticationHooks: Banner grammar: a seed composes layout, button hierarchy, copy tone and about a dozen trap modules (hidden reject, confirmshaming, pre-ticked toggles, inverted switches, resetting countdown, fake close, cookie wall, nested vendor list, re-prompt); a breadth-first solver over each banner's state machine proves the room is solvable and computes par and the friction ratio.
Fair-trap rule: every trick carries a visible tell, and an assist mode, which doubles as the accessible path for keyboard and screen-reader players, narrates the tell in plain words.

Bestiary and debrief teach the named patterns and a real-world cheat sheet, so the quiet payoff is spotting the same tricks on real sites; dated study figures sit in the about panel beside their sources.

Roguelike layer and bends: quicksand rooms where each refusal opens another layer, an obsidian dark theme for the boss, a vendor list of hundreds of outposts, relics, a patience meter, a daily seed and a spoiler-free share receipt in the URL hash.
design.scopeForOneDay: Built in the morning: the banner engine (spec, renderer, three visual themes, about twelve trap modules), the breadth-first solver for par and friction ratio, a run of eight rooms plus a boss, relics, bestiary, assist mode, daily seed and share receipt, and an about panel with dated sources. Cut: real-site lookalikes, any network call, audio beyond UI clicks, accounts and leaderboards.
risks: Prior art: a Swiss broadcaster's browser game, a thesis game and similar teaching games exist. Planned mitigation: a credit line in the about panel and a pitch built on procedural variety, solver-checked par and the friction ratio rather than on the premise.
Accessibility: a game about hidden buttons can exclude people, so full keyboard play and the assist mode belong in the core spec, not the stretch list.

Safety framing: every site, brand and banner is invented and labelled parody; no real logos, no legal claims about real sites and no data collection; the page sets no cookies and says so, with localStorage used only for a best result inside try/catch.
Preachiness and repetition: the page needs a narrator with real jokes and enough copy and mutators that room ten still surprises, so copy writing starts first.

Unverified details: the five-category typology and the pointsification critique rest on blended or single results and appear only as 'as of 2026-10-11, per the named source' or not at all; the 11.8% figure is shown as 'in the study's sample' because the denominator is unclear.
